prompt: In a table-driven test, what does adding a new case usually cost?

choices.text: A new `Test` function with its own setup
choices.why: That is what the table replaces: the setup is written once, in the loop.

choices.text: One row
choices.why: Right. `only punctuation` and `digits` were one line each.

choices.text: A new subtest written by hand inside the loop
choices.why: The loop calls `t.Run` once per row; nothing is written inside it per case.

choices.text: A change to the anonymous struct's fields
choices.why: The fields change only when a new kind of thing starts to vary between cases.

prompt: Why does the table compare the whole map with `maps.Equal` rather than checking a few words as lesson 25 did?
hint: What would a `Count` that also produced a stray `fun.` do to each kind of check?

choices.text: Because indexing a map in a test is not allowed
choices.why: Lesson 25 indexed the map in every check, and those tests compiled and ran.

choices.text: Because `maps.Equal` is faster
choices.why: Speed is not the point for maps of a handful of words.

choices.text: It catches a word the test did not ask about
choices.why: Right. Checking `fun` alone passes a map that also holds a wrong `fun.`; comparing all of it does not.

choices.text: Because a table row cannot hold more than one expectation
choices.why: A row may hold as many fields as the cases need.

prompt: A teammate wants to fold `TestCountFile` into the `TestCount` table with a `file bool` column. What does the lesson say against it?
hint: Do all the rows go through the same steps?

choices.text: A case with its own steps is its own test
choices.why: Right. Every other row would carry a field it ignores, and the loop an `if` for one case.

choices.text: Tables cannot contain `bool` fields
choices.why: A struct field can be of any type; the objection is about steps, not types.

choices.text: `t.TempDir` does not work inside a subtest of the table
choices.why: It works in any test or subtest; each gets its own directory.

choices.text: Files are slower to read than strings
choices.why: The section's argument is about the shape of the test, not its speed.

prompt: Before Go 1.22, a table loop that started closures copied its row first with the line `tc ___ tc`.
A row is named `only punctuation`. Under what name does the report show its subtest?

choices.text: `TestCount/only punctuation`
choices.why: The space does not survive into the reported name.

choices.text: `TestCount/"only punctuation"`
choices.why: No quotes are added; the name is rewritten instead.

choices.text: `TestCount/6`
choices.why: Rows are not numbered; the `name` field is used.

choices.text: `TestCount/only_punctuation`
choices.why: Right: the space becomes an underscore.

prompt: `go test -v -run 'TestCount/only punctuation'` also ran `TestCountFile` in full. Why?
hint: What does the first level of the pattern match?

choices.text: Because a space in a `-run` pattern matches any test
choices.why: The space is rewritten to an underscore and matched normally; `only_punctuation` was the only row of `TestCount` that ran.

choices.text: The first level is not anchored
choices.why: Right, and `TestCountFile` has no subtests for the second level to filter. `^TestCount$` fixes it.

choices.text: Because `go test` always runs every test that uses `t.TempDir`
choices.why: Nothing about `t.TempDir` affects which tests are selected.

choices.text: Because `-v` disables `-run`
choices.why: `-v` changes the output, not the selection; `TestCount` ran only one row.

prompt: Why is `case 3` a poor name for a row, beyond saying nothing about the case?
hint: What happens to the numbers when a row is inserted above it?

choices.text: Digits are not allowed in subtest names
choices.why: They are allowed; the report would print `TestCount/case_3`.

choices.text: Names with numbers run in numeric order
choices.why: Subtests run in the order of the table, whatever their names.

choices.text: An insert moves the numbers away from the rows
choices.why: Right. A name tied to position stops naming the case the day the table changes.

choices.text: It collides with `go test -count=3`
choices.why: `-count` repeats runs; it has nothing to do with names.

prompt: A case fails on machines without a network and the cause is being worked on. Why does the lesson prefer `t.Skip` to commenting the row out?
hint: Which of the two still appears in every report?

choices.text: A commented-out row makes the file fail to compile
choices.why: A comment compiles fine; that is exactly why it is easy to forget.

choices.text: A skip stays in the report, with its reason
choices.why: Right. A commented row vanishes from everybody's view; a skip is reported on every run.

choices.text: `t.Skip` makes the test pass, which keeps CI green
choices.why: It ends the test as skipped, not passed, and says why.

choices.text: `t.Skip` retries the case until the network returns
choices.why: It does not retry anything; it ends the test there.

prompt: Which failure message follows the Go convention?
hint: Call, then what it returned, then what was wanted.

choices.text: `wrong result`
choices.why: It names neither the call, the input, nor either value.

choices.text: `expected 4 entries`
choices.why: It gives the expectation without what came back or what was called.

choices.text: `Top(counts, 4) = [{is 3} {go 3}], want [{go 3} {is 3}]`
choices.why: Right: the call as made, `=`, what it returned, `want` and the expectation.

choices.text: `want [{go 3} {is 3}] but got something else entirely`
choices.why: Without the value that came back, the reader has to rerun the test to see it.

prompt: In twenty runs of the buggy `TestTop`, in how many did the `first` row fail?
Why did the buggy `Top` return tied words in a different order from run to run?
hint: Where did the slice's starting order come from?

choices.text: `slices.SortFunc` shuffles its input before sorting
choices.why: The sort is deterministic for a given input; the input itself changed.

choices.text: Map order is random and ties kept it
choices.why: Right. Ties kept whatever order the map produced, and that order changes on purpose.

choices.text: The goroutines in `Top` raced
choices.why: `Top` starts no goroutine.

choices.text: `cmp.Compare` returns a random sign for equal values
choices.why: It returns 0 for equal values, and the sort is then free to keep any order the input had.

prompt: You run `go test .` twice and the second run prints `(cached)`. You then change a file `Count` reads from disk, outside the package. What does a third `go test .` do?
hint: The cache is keyed on the code and the test. What else could a test depend on?

choices.text: It fails, because the cache detects any changed file on the machine
choices.why: The lesson says the cache tracks the code and the test, not every file on the machine.

choices.text: It refuses to run until `go clean` is used
choices.why: Nothing refuses; a cached pass is simply replayed.

choices.text: It reruns, because a third run always bypasses the cache
choices.why: There is no such rule; the cache is replayed as long as the code and test are unchanged.

choices.text: It replays the cached pass; `-count=1` would rerun it
choices.why: Right. A test depending on something outside the package is exactly when to reach for `-count=1`.

prompt: Match each comparison with what it suits.
hint: Three come from packages, one is an operator.

pairs.right: any two values, nested ones included
a struct whose fields are all comparable

right_distractors: two goroutines' views of one variable

prompt: Put the parts of a Go failure message in the conventional order.
hint: It reads like the call itself.

prompt: A table test passes on your laptop and fails one run in ten on CI, always on a row whose expected slice was built from a map. What is the first thing to suspect?

choices.text: The CI machine has a different number of processors
choices.why: Nothing in a map walk depends on processors; the randomisation is per run, on any machine.

choices.text: An order that comes from walking a map, which Go randomises
choices.why: Right. It changes between identical runs; either the code imposes an order or the test stops depending on one.

choices.text: A stale `(cached)` result on the laptop
choices.why: A cache would show the same verdict every time, not one failure in ten on CI.

choices.text: A missing `t.Helper()` in the loop
choices.why: `t.Helper` changes which line a failure names, not whether it happens.

prompt: Which of these belong in the table, as rows of `TestCount`? Choose all that apply.
hint: A row goes through the same steps as the others.

choices.text: A text with a tab between two words
choices.why: Yes: another input and its expected map.

choices.text: A text in Portuguese with `não` and `NÃO`
choices.why: Yes: same steps, different data.

choices.text: Counting a file that does not exist
choices.why: That needs a file system and an error check, which is `TestCountFile`'s job.

choices.text: Checking `Top` returns ties alphabetically
choices.why: Different function, different steps: that is `TestTop`.
